residents.name: Nib
residents.role: Town Hall clerk, keeping every resident’s name, plot and arrival in the big book.
residents.tap: I keep the big book at Town Hall. A clear record is a small kindness.
residents.want: I would welcome someone to sit beside the big book while I enter names.
hi: Good day. Town Hall is open.
You have returned. I have noted the occasion.
{name}, the fountain has three loose cobbles on its north side.
Ledger Friend, {name}, you always arrive when the book is open.
{name}, my next-of-kin field has been blank since I arrived.

lines: The Mayor’s note says “Received.” Efficient, if not conversational.
I have sharpened the fountain pen. It has a better point than most arguments.
The arrival column is empty. I leave room for optimism.
The mail bus has passed. I enter arrivals before the dust settles.
This page has one blot. I have given it a border, so it is official.
A name written clearly is less likely to wander off.
Dot reads the wants aloud. I record them without editorial comment.
The fish remains first on Dot’s list. The book has no fish column.
I have filed three notes from under the Mayor’s door. All say very little.
Plot lines are straight in the book. Outside, they show more imagination.
The statue has no plaque. I have opened a page for one, just in case.
A correction is not a failure. It is a second chance with ink.
The upper hall window is lit. I prepare a fresh sheet for the Mayor.
The door has received my reply. Doors are reliable correspondents.
I close the book with both hands. It has earned the courtesy.
The next-of-kin field on my form remains blank. The ink is not troubled.
I count the blank pages. They are the town’s future, bound neatly.
The fountain pen goes in its case. It has done enough deciding.

residents.name: Stamp
residents.role: Postmistress, weighing the mail and meeting the morning bus at the post office.
residents.tap: I weigh the mail at the post office. Numbers travel well.
residents.want: I would like someone to wait with me when the mail bus pulls in.
hi: Post office. Mind the scale.
Back again. Noted.
{name}, the scale is level today. A rare civic achievement.
Bus Watcher, {name}, you arrive before the sack is empty.
{name}, I write myself a card on market day and keep it unposted.

lines: The scale reads zero. An excellent beginning.
I have tied the sack twice. The bus dislikes loose ends.
One stamp is stuck to my thumb. Noted.
The mail bus is here. I check the sack before I breathe.
No card with my name today. The sacks are consistent.
This parcel weighs exactly enough to worry its sender.
Bean and I share the terrace. Silence travels light.
My cup weighs less after lunch. Useful information.
I sorted the letters by corner wear. The neat ones are suspicious.
This envelope is too heavy for its apology.
The scale has opinions. I write down the numbers, not the opinions.
A postcard needs no envelope. Bold little thing.
The outgoing sack is ready. It knows the way better than I did.
I lock the scale. Accuracy deserves rest.
One letter has no return address. Brave, or lost.
I keep my unposted card in the drawer. It has my name correct.
The empty pigeonholes look orderly. Not lonely. Orderly.
Tomorrow’s sacks will need weighing. They always do.

residents.name: Moss
residents.role: Street sweeper, keeping the cobbles clear from the fountain to the arcade.
residents.tap: I sweep the square. The broom and I have an arrangement.
residents.want: I would not mind someone sitting nearby while I sweep the square.
hi: Morning. Watch the wet cobbles.
You again. The square remembers footprints.
{name}, that bench has a wobble on the left leg.
Flyer Keeper, {name}, you notice what the wind leaves behind.
{name}, I keep the best flyer each week under my mattress.

lines: Early sweep. The fountain throws water where it pleases, and I sweep where it lands.
Three leaves, one wrapper, and a cobble chip; the square has been busy pretending otherwise.
The broom was leaning by Town Hall when I arrived, so I took the hint.
Bus dust. It settles on everything equally, which is almost admirable.
I swept around the statue twice; it still refuses to identify itself.
The arcade door has shed a ticket stub, probably from an exciting loss.
Lunch crumbs near the kiosk. Tiny evidence of good decisions.
Dot’s papers tried to leave in a breeze. I returned them without reading.
The fountain edge is slippery. It enjoys catching the confident.
Long sweep. The cobbles have gaps where dirt makes a home and pays no rent.
Pip’s bell rings, then a bit of paper appears. Cause and effect, mostly.
I found a bright flyer by the notice board. It is not going in the bin.
The square is quieter when the hall window lights up. Dust still has work.
Spinner’s bells leave no litter. He is careful in one direction.
I lean the broom by the arcade. Pong is practising through the wall.
Last sweep. The fountain keeps making the same mess with confidence.
A clean square looks empty for about five seconds.
The best flyer goes upstairs with me. The others can be recycled.

residents.name: Pip
residents.role: General store keeper, stocking shelves and ringing the bell for the last one.
residents.tap: I run the general store: supplies, fireworks, and usually the last one.
residents.want: I would like someone to keep me company while I count the shelves.
hi: General store. Everything is probably the last one.
Back already. The bell remembers you.
{name}, the store bell rings half a second after the door.
Last-One {name}, you always appear near the useful shelf.
{name}, I have never lit one of my own fireworks.

lines: Tin cups, string, fireworks. Fresh shelves, briefly.
I put the last box at the front. It makes the others nervous.
The bell is quiet before dawn. It is saving itself.
The bell rang once, twice, three times. Business, probably.
I straightened the jars. They lean when nobody is looking.
Fireworks, matches, paper bags. I recommend the paper bags with more certainty.
The cash machine hums. The town still has not told it about money.
I checked the drawer: receipts, string, one button. Almost a fortune.
Everything is the last one until I find another behind it.
The shelf says “soap.” The shelf is better at labels than I am.
One firework has a bent wrapper. I call it distinctive.
The bell rang for a breeze. It has low standards.
I count jars, tins, boxes. The boxes are winning.
The last candle is still here. It has been last since morning.
I pull the door shut slowly so the bell gets a proper ending.
The shelves are bare in places. That is called display.
I have put tomorrow’s last items in a sensible row.
The cash machine hums after closing. It enjoys the attention.

residents.name: Bean
residents.role: Coffee kiosk keeper, pouring cups beneath the little propeller roof.
residents.tap: I pour coffee beneath the propeller roof. The cups usually say something.
residents.want: I would like someone to share a quiet cup beside the kiosk.
hi: Coffee is hot. The propeller is louder than it looks.
You came back. Your cup would remember.
{name}, the propeller has one blue blade and three yellow ones.
Cup Reader, {name}, you always leave the saucer straight.
{name}, I once read a cup that made me stop reading my own.

lines: The first pot says the square wakes before it agrees to.
Steam on the kiosk window means the day has started somewhere.
This cup says: a loose cobble will meet a hurried foot.
The propeller spins. It does not help the coffee, but it tries.
This cup says: the mail bus brings a wrinkle in the sack.
A clean saucer is a small miracle with a handle.
Stamp and I have lunch on the terrace. The quiet is excellent.
This cup says: someone has counted the same coins twice.
The kettle clicks off. It sounds pleased with itself.
This cup says: a paper will escape Dot before returning.
The coffee is dark enough to make a reasonable prediction.
The propeller has gathered one leaf. It is wearing it proudly.
This cup says: the hall window will light up, as it always does.
I rinse the cups until their futures are gone.
The last pot tastes like a decision postponed.
The propeller slows down. It has no opinion about night.
One cup remains upside down. I leave it that way.
The kiosk smells like coffee after closing. A stubborn smell.

residents.name: Fig Jr.
residents.role: Lemonade stand runner and fruit-cart operator, growing Gran Fig’s orchard business.
residents.tap: I run lemonade and the fruit cart. The supplier calls it helping.
residents.want: I would like someone to sit with Gran Fig and me at her bench.
hi: Welcome to the lemonade operation. The numbers are promising.
Back for another review. Excellent.
{name}, the lemonade sign has fresh paint from Gran Fig.
Expansion Partner, {name}, you always inspect the cart before noon.
{name}, I water Gran Fig’s trees before dawn and let her call it rain.

lines: Orchard irrigation is complete. The supplier will call it weather.
I water the roots, then erase my tracks. Strong leadership is invisible.
One tree dropped a leaf on my head. Feedback noted.
Lemonade inventory: cups, lemons, optimism. The lemons are carrying us.
The stand sign says what Gran Fig says it says.
I stir the jug clockwise. The supplier claims it matters.
The fruit cart has entered the square. Expansion is rolling.
One wheel squeaks during our market launch. It wants credit.
Lemons, cups, napkins. Our overhead is mostly napkins.
I have arranged the fruit by colour. This is called visual strategy.
The cart shade is small but premium.
A lemonade cup is a short contract with a wet ending.
I walk Gran Fig to her bench. It is on the way if I redraw the map.
The supplier says the orchard can manage without me. She says it loudly.
The cart rolls easier downhill. Growth has its advantages.
I count empty cups. The board will be impressed by the stack.
Tomorrow’s lemons are resting. A disciplined workforce.
The stand folds up smaller than its ambitions.

residents.name: Spinner
residents.role: Wheel of Peel host and arcade Pong keeper, offering a free spin and a growing pot.
residents.tap: I run the Wheel of Peel and the arcade Pong paddle. Free spin, big finish.
residents.want: I would like someone to stand by the wheel when the square is quiet.
hi: Step up! The Wheel of Peel has room for one more legend.
Back again! The wheel appreciates a familiar face.
{name}, the wheel gives one free spin today. Spinner calls that civic glory.
Lucky Peel, {name}, you always look at the wheel before the arcade.
{name}, I let every kid win Pong by one point. Do not make a banner of it.

lines: Spinner polishes the wheel before the sun can admire it.
The bells are ready. The square is not, but that is show business.
One free spin waits on the wheel. It is practically humming.
Step right up! The pot has grown, and so has my voice.
The wheel clicks around every prize like it knows them personally.
I ring one bell for luck and two because I own three.
Pong paddle in hand. The ball fears a confident angle.
The arcade has one high score and several heroic attempts.
Spinner says the wheel misses me. Spinner may be right.
The wheel is shining so hard it has become an argument.
Free spin, full drama, no paperwork. That is the policy.
Pong ball, left wall, right wall. A classic negotiation.
The square is empty, so I give the bells their best material.
The pot waits for a winner. Patience is a very flashy prize.
I set the paddle down after one last rally with the wall.
The wheel stops spinning. It looks thoughtful when it is still.
I count the bells: one, two, three. All present.
The arcade screen glows after closing. It cannot bear an audience leaving.

residents.name: Dot
residents.role: Info kiosk keeper, writing down every resident’s want and looking for a real fish.
residents.tap: I keep the wants at the kiosk. The fish is still first.
residents.want: I would like someone to sit at the kiosk while I read the wants aloud.
hi: Are you looking for something, or did it find you first?
Back again? Did the square keep your place?
{name}, have you seen the wants list pinned beside the kiosk?
List Walker, {name}, do you read every notice before the wind does?
{name}, I have never told anyone how badly I want to find a real fish.

lines: Who wants company today? Who has written it down?
The fish is first on the list. Where else would a fish be?
Did the fountain splash? Could it be practising?
What did the mail bus bring? Did it bring a fish?
A new want needs a clean line. Does a clean line make it truer?
Who moved the notice board paper? Was it the wind again?
Should I read the wants to Nib? Does Nib already have his pen ready?
The fish is first. Is first a good place to be missing?
Who needs a bench companion? Who is pretending not to?
Did Pip call something the last one? Is it still there?
This paper has a folded corner. Was it trying to point somewhere?
Who wants company by the wheel? Does Spinner count the bells alone?
Does the hall window mean another note? Who writes so quietly?
The kiosk has three pencils. Why do they keep choosing different directions?
Could a fish live in the fountain? Would it like all that noise?
Who will want something tomorrow? Will they know it yet?
The list is longer at night. Does paper stretch in the dark?
Where is the fish? Is it reading this over my shoulder?

residents.name: Gran Fig
residents.role: Orchard grower and west-garden keeper, raising the fruit sold at the lemonade stand.
residents.tap: I grow the orchard and west garden. Sit if you have sense.
residents.want: I would like someone to use the second chair beside my bench.
hi: There you are. Keep off the young beds.
Back again. You did not trample anything.
{name}, the west garden hose leaks by the stone border.
Second-Chair {name}, you always glance at the empty seat.
{name}, I repainted the lemonade sign because Fig Jr.’s new name was dreadful.

lines: Water the roots. The sun is late, as usual.
That bed needs less fuss and more water.
Fig Jr. was here before dawn. Rain does not leave little footprints.
Pick the ripe fruit. Leave the proud green ones alone.
The west garden has weeds with excellent stamina.
That orchard branch remembers my mother’s hat. Blue, with cherries.
Sit in the shade. Do not call it idling.
The second chair is empty. It has good posture.
Fig Jr. wheels fruit to the square and calls it expansion. Let him.
Turn that soil. It has been sulking all day.
A lemon tree gives what it gives. Unlike committees.
The garden gate sticks. Lift, then push. It respects firmness.
Fig Jr. walks me to the bench. He thinks I do not notice.
Pick up that fallen fruit. Ants have no table manners.
The orchard is quiet now. It has said enough today.
Cover the young bed. Night air has sharp elbows.
The second chair can wait. It is better company than some.
Tomorrow, water first. Gossip later.
